subject: Grouping: most-common-value and percentile aggregates, dropping missing keys, top rows per group
brief:
Additions to grouping in the tabula aggregate module.

1. A new aggregate name `common`, listed in AGGREGATES with the others: the most frequent value of the group, ignoring None. Edge case: when several values are equally frequent, the one that appears first in the group wins (not the smallest one). A group without any present value gives None.
2. Percentile aggregate names: a lower-case p followed by a whole number from 0 to 100, written without leading zeros, is that percentile of the group's values, ignoring None, computed with the same linear interpolation as `stats.quantile` (so the 50th percentile of four numbers is the mean of the middle two, and the 0th and 100th percentiles are the minimum and the maximum). A group without numbers gives None. Any other spelling (a number above 100, no number, a leading zero, a fraction, a sign, another letter, an upper-case P) is an unknown aggregate and raises ValueError, as unknown names already do. These names are not entries of AGGREGATES, but they work wherever an aggregate name is accepted: in `group_by` and in `pivot`.
3. `group_by` takes a keyword `dropna` (default False). When it is true, rows that have None in any of the key columns are left out entirely; by default such rows still form their own group as before.
4. A new function `top_n(table, keys, column, n, largest=True)` in the aggregate module: for every group of `keys` (one name or a list; groups in order of first appearance, a None key being a group of its own), the rows with the n largest values of `column` (the smallest when `largest` is false), best first, with all columns kept. Rows with equal values keep their original relative order, in both directions. Rows whose value is None are never chosen, so a group can contribute fewer than n rows, or none at all. n below 1 or an empty key list raises ValueError; an unknown column raises KeyError.

All behavior that the existing tests check must keep working.
